newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch royal visit to S Africa seals reconciliation.
newsitem.headline: Dutch royal visit to S Africa seals reconciliation.

text.p: Next week's visit by Queen Beatrix to South Africa will set the royal seal of approval on the Netherlands' reconciliation with its former colony after decades of apartheid rule.

The Queen's four-day trip at the invitation of president Nelson Mandela marks the first-ever state visit by a Dutch monarch to South Africa in more than three centuries of often stormy bilateral relations.
"Before the Second World War the journey was too arduous to make a royal visit feasible; after the war the political situation made it impossible," said a government historian.

The lush vineyards and gabled farmhouses fringing Cape Town's urban sprawl are present-day reminders of the city's origins as a refreshment station for 17th century Dutch mariners bound for the spice islands of the Indies.
Links between the Dutch and their former colonists were particularly close in the late 1890s when the Dutch rallied behind the Afrikaaners during the Boer Wars against the British.
The then Queen, Wilhelmina, dispatched a Dutch warship to the Transvaal to fetch defeated Boer leader Paul Kruger, who arrived in the Netherlands to a hero's welcome.

But in more recent times both countries chose to ignore rather than embrace their common heritage, driven apart by the policy of legally enforced segregation imposed by South Africa's ruling Nationalist Party in 1948.

Queen Beatrix's German-born father Prince Bernhard publicly spoke out against apartheid during an informal trade visit to South Africa in 1954. And in 1960 the Dutch government condemned apartheid after the Sharpeville massacre of 69 black demonstrators.
Over the next two decades the Netherlands led international opposition to the Pretoria regime, lobbying fiercely for European measures to underwrite U.N. Security Council sanctions.
At home, Prime Minister Dries van Agt's Christian Democrat-led coalition government drafted a bill to ban Dutch investment in South Africa, but lost power before it became law.
Fuelled by a series of high-profile media campaigns urging a boycott of South African produce, Dutch public opposition to apartheid erupted into violence in the early 1980s.
An anti-racism guerrilla group torched a string of Shell petrol stations in protest at the Anglo-Dutch petroleum giant's refusal to pull out of South Africa.
Royal Dutch/Shell held firm, but a spate of similar attacks on its cash-and-carry outlets forced privately-owned retail multinational SHV Makro to shut up shop in South Africa in 1987.

In March SHV announced it had returned, pumping millions of dollars into its previously-divested Makro South Africa. But other Dutch companies have been slow to follow since sanctions were lifted in 1990.
The Netherlands now ranks ninth in the South African league table of foreign investment, he says, with total assets worth some 470 million dollars.
As such they trail Britain in first place and -- more surprisingly -- Belgium in eighth place. "Dutch entrepreneurs have tended to take a wait-and-see approach," Matthijsse says.
But the ministry sees Dutch investment picking up over the next few years.

Economic affairs minister Hans Wijers will take a trade mission to South Africa to coincide with the Queen's visit. Companies taking part include banks ABN AMRO and ING, national airline KLM and post and telecoms group Dutch PTT.
Queen Beatrix will be accompanied on the September 30- October 3 visit by consort Prince Claus and heir to the throne Prince Willem Alexander.
The royals will start their four-city tour in Pretoria on Monday with a reception hosted by Mandela and on Tuesday the Queen will open an exhibition of Dutch Old Masters in Johannesburg.
The official part of the stay will end in Cape Town with a reception in the original fort built by the Dutch East India Company. The royals will stay on in Cape Town for a holiday.
